slides.title: What XSS is
slides.summary: XSS happens when attacker-controlled data ends up running as code in your page, with all of your origin's power.
body: Cross-site scripting is still the most common frontend vulnerability. The attacker gets the browser to treat their text as HTML or JavaScript inside your page.
Once their script runs, it is your app as far as the browser is concerned. It can:

ul: read the page, including personal data and CSRF tokens;
read localStorage and any token you keep there;
make authenticated requests as the user (change email, transfer money);
rewrite the page to show a fake login form.

body: <mark>Any place where data becomes markup or code is a possible XSS sink.</mark>

steps.caption: The payload is stored as ordinary text.
The developer used innerHTML to support bold text.
The image fails to load, so its error handler runs.
Every reader of the comment is now compromised.

slides.title: What an attacker can do with XSS
slides.summary: Once their script runs in your page, attackers can steal sessions, act as the user, record keystrokes, read data and fake your UI.
body: Take a recipe site that shows each cook's display name with innerHTML. An attacker sets their name to a payload, and every visitor who opens one of their recipes runs it. From there:

ul: Session hijacking: read any cookie that isn't HttpOnly, or a token in localStorage, and send it to the attacker's server.
Actions as the user: call your own APIs with the user's session: post spam, change the email address, delete the account.
Keylogging: listen to keydown on the whole page and send what the user types, including passwords on the next form they fill in.
Data theft: copy document.body.innerHTML, which can include saved addresses, orders or messages.
Phishing inside your page: inject a fake “Session expired, please sign in” form that posts the password to the attacker. The address bar still shows your domain, so users trust it.

body: <mark>An XSS bug gives the attacker everything your own JavaScript can do. That's why it's treated as critical.</mark>

body.note: Payloads rarely need a <script> tag. Event handlers (onerror, onfocus with autofocus), <svg onload> and javascript: URLs all run code, so filtering the word “script” protects nothing.

cells.text: Only by preventing the XSS (encode, sanitize, CSP)

viz.html: Some defences limit the damage; only preventing the injection stops all of it.

slides.title: Three kinds of XSS
slides.summary: Stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS differ in where the payload travels. The fix is the same: never let data become code.

ul: Stored: the payload is saved (a comment, a profile name) and served to every viewer.
Reflected: the payload is in the request, usually the URL, and the server echoes it into the page.
DOM-based: the payload never reaches the server. Client code reads it from location, postMessage or storage and writes it into the DOM.

body: <mark>Single-page apps mostly face DOM-based XSS, because the client does the rendering.</mark>

body.note: Server-side scanners and logs often can't see DOM XSS: everything after the # in a URL is never sent to the server.

blocks.title: Profile name saved in the DB

figure.alt: Three lanes. Stored XSS: an attacker posts a comment containing a script, the database stores it, the app renders it as HTML, and it runs for every viewer. Reflected XSS: the attacker sends a crafted link with the payload in the query string, the server echoes it into the HTML response, and it runs for whoever clicks the link. DOM-based XSS: the payload is in the URL fragment after the hash, which never reaches the server; client JavaScript reads location.hash and writes it into innerHTML, and it runs in the victim's tab. Each lane ends in a red box: the script runs with your origin's privileges.

slides.title: Encode for the context
slides.summary: Text APIs keep data as data. HTML APIs parse it. Escape for exactly where the data lands.
body: The main defence is output encoding: turn special characters into harmless text for the context the data is written into.

ul: HTML text: use textContent or your framework's text binding, never innerHTML.
Attributes: set them with setAttribute or bindings; never build event-handler attributes (onclick) from data.
URLs: parse with new URL() and allow only https:, http: and mailto:. A javascript: URL in an href runs code on click.
Inside <script>: don't. Pass data as JSON in a data- attribute or a type="application/json" block.

body: <mark>Frameworks escape text bindings for you. XSS in modern apps almost always comes through an escape hatch.</mark>

viz.html: Search your codebase for the right-hand column. Each hit needs a reason and a review.

figure.alt: The same untrusted string, , is written into the page in two ways. On the left, el.textContent = input: the browser shows the characters literally on screen and nothing runs. On the right, el.innerHTML = input: the browser parses it, creates an image element, the image fails to load, and its onerror handler runs steal() in your origin.

slides.title: When you must render HTML
slides.summary: Sanitize with a maintained sanitizer, then lock the sinks with Trusted Types and a strict CSP.
body: Rich text, Markdown and CMS content need real HTML. Don't write your own filter: regex blocklists are bypassed all the time.

ul: Sanitize with an allowlist of tags and attributes: DOMPurify, Angular's built-in sanitizer, or the browser's new setHTML().
Sanitize as late as possible, just before inserting, so nothing changes the HTML afterwards.
Turn on Trusted Types so the browser rejects plain strings at innerHTML and other sinks. It has worked in all major browsers since early 2026.
Add a strict CSP so that if a payload gets through, it still doesn't run.

body: <mark>Trusted Types turns “find every innerHTML in the codebase” into “review a few policy functions”.</mark>

body.text: el.setHTML(html) parses and sanitizes in one step, using the browser's own parser, so there's no mismatch between how the sanitizer and the browser read the HTML. Firefox 148 shipped it in February 2026; check support in other browsers before relying on it, and keep DOMPurify as the fallback.

body.more: CSP and Trusted Types in depth
body.text: The Security headers chapter covers the CSP side.

code: // One reviewed policy; every other innerHTML write now throws.

figure.alt: Two paths into innerHTML under a Trusted Types policy. Top path: code passes a plain string straight to innerHTML; the browser throws a TypeError and sends a CSP violation report, so nothing is inserted. Bottom path: code passes the string through a named policy, whose createHTML function calls a sanitizer such as DOMPurify and returns a TrustedHTML object; innerHTML accepts it. Because only policies can create trusted values, a security review only needs to look at the few policy functions instead of every innerHTML call.

slides.title: XSS defence checklist
slides.summary: A layered checklist: find every input, keep data as text, sanitize when HTML is unavoidable, never evaluate strings, and back it all with CSP.

ul: Inventory every input: form fields, URL query and hash, postMessage, storage, third-party APIs, file names, even HTTP headers you echo back.
Render as text: framework bindings or textContent. Treat innerHTML and its relatives as code review red flags.
Encode for the context when you build markup on the server: HTML body, attribute, URL and JavaScript contexts each need different escaping.
Sanitize when HTML is required: DOMPurify, Angular's sanitizer or setHTML(), with an allowlist.
Never evaluate strings: no eval, new Function, or setTimeout / setInterval with a string.
Validate URLs before putting them in href or src.
Defence in depth: strict CSP with nonces, Trusted Types, HttpOnly cookies, and no secrets in the page.

body: <mark>Encoding and sanitizing prevent XSS. CSP and Trusted Types make the bugs you miss far less harmful.</mark>

body.text: Directives, fallbacks, nonces and rollout are covered in the Security headers chapter.
